stages.title: Make room to contribute
stages.explanation: The group asks for everyone’s ideas, then votes before reading half of them. Participation has become a suggestion box with a very efficient lid. A leadership move gives someone a workable way to influence a decision. Offer a route they can accept or decline, then watch what happens to their contribution. An invitation is a start; its effect still needs checking.
modelRows: Invite
“Would you sketch a layout, or would you prefer to comment on ours?” A choice gives the teammate a way in.
Observe
The teammate sketches a larger title. The group uses it on the final poster.
Interpret
You can report what changed on the poster. To know how the teammate felt, ask them.
stages.model:
Invite — “Would you sketch a layout, or would you prefer to comment on ours?” A choice gives the teammate a way in.
Observe — The teammate sketches a larger title. The group uses it on the final poster.
Interpret — You can report what changed on the poster. To know how the teammate felt, ask them.

questions.prompt: Which invitation gives a real choice?
options: You must explain the poster to everyone.
Would you rather sketch an idea or review our two designs?
answers: Would you rather sketch an idea or review our two designs?
questions.hint: Can the teammate choose how to contribute?
questions.explanation: Both routes let the teammate influence the design.

alternate.prompt: Which invitation fits a planning meeting?
options: Would you like to add an idea aloud or leave a written suggestion?
You have to go first.
answers: Would you like to add an idea aloud or leave a written suggestion?

questions.prompt: Which detail is observable evidence of influence?
options: Everyone felt valued.
The leader meant well.
The group used the teammate’s larger title.
answers: The group used the teammate’s larger title.
questions.hint: What could another observer check?
questions.explanation: The final design contains the suggestion.

alternate.prompt: Which fact shows an idea reached the plan?
options: The speaker felt proud.
The final schedule includes the break they proposed.
answers: The final schedule includes the break they proposed.

rehearsal.prompt: A teammate prefers drawing to speaking. Complete the invitation with one real alternative: “Would you like to sketch a layout, or _____?”
rehearsal.sample: Would you like to sketch a layout, or comment on the two layouts we already have? Either route can influence the choice.

image.alt: A leader collects idea cards; later the group examines them and includes a distinctive spiral from a card in its final poster.
image.caption: Trace the spiral from suggestion to final design: that change is observable evidence of influence. Collecting a card alone is not. AI-generated teaching illustration.

stages.title: Interpret and adjust
stages.explanation: “Everyone felt included” would be lovely. Unless you asked, it is also a guess. Report what you could observe: a suggestion was used, a card stayed unread, or someone declined. Then adjust the part you can control. An invitation that falls flat is useful evidence, not a reason to invent a happy ending.
modelRows: Action
A facilitator asks for written ideas before a vote.
Observation
Three cards appear. The group votes before reading two of them.
Adjustment
Read every card before the next vote. Collecting ideas gave people a turn; the order of the vote limited their influence.
stages.model:
Action — A facilitator asks for written ideas before a vote.
Observation — Three cards appear. The group votes before reading two of them.
Adjustment — Read every card before the next vote. Collecting ideas gave people a turn; the order of the vote limited their influence.

questions.prompt: Which adjustment responds to those two unread cards?
options: Ask for five cards next time.
Read all submissions before opening the vote.
answers: Read all submissions before opening the vote.
questions.hint: At what point did influence break down?
questions.explanation: The issue came after collection and before the decision.

alternate.prompt: A leader invites questions after people have left. What adjustment fits?
options: Reserve question time before dismissal.
Print more invitations.
answers: Reserve question time before dismissal.

rehearsal.prompt: You invited a quiet teammate to choose a task. They picked checking sources, but nobody waited for the check. Write one adjustment linked to what happened.
rehearsal.sample: I would reserve two minutes for their source check before we submit, so their work can affect the final answer.

questions.prompt: A teammate declines an invitation. Which reflection fits the evidence?
options: They have no ideas.
They declined this time; offer another route without assuming why.
answers: They declined this time; offer another route without assuming why.
questions.hint: Separate an observed response from a guessed motive.
questions.explanation: A refusal gives information about this moment, not a private motive.

alternate.prompt: A suggestion receives no reply. Which note is accurate?
options: They all disliked it.
There was no reply before the topic changed.
answers: There was no reply before the topic changed.

final.title: Try one move and report what happened
final.source: Use an actual group task. If you are together now, take two minutes with a consenting partner to choose a name or layout for a class event (choose either task). Invite a contribution in a way they can accept or decline. Notice what happened to the decision. If working alone, plan your move now and return after the next group task to submit. Omit names.
final.prompt: After trying the move, write 3–5 sentences: What was your shared goal? What did you actually say or do? What did someone do in response, and what effect, if any, did that have? Explain one adjustment for next time. An unsuccessful invitation is valid evidence.
rubric: Action: Describes an enacted move toward a shared goal. A future plan or hypothetical scenario alone needs a follow-up after practice.
Observation: Describes an observable response and its effect or lack of effect on the group, without requiring names or a successful outcome.
Reflection: Connects a feasible adjustment to the observed result. Assess the written reflection as self-report, without claiming independent observation.
final.delayedCheck: At the next group task, try your adjustment in a new decision. Record what someone actually did and whether it changed the result. Compare that observation with your expectation.

title: Symbol and Allegory in The Alchemist
objective: Explain how a concrete symbol and two connected events in The Alchemist develop a broader idea about pursuing a purpose.

stages.title: A sheep is still a sheep—and can suggest more
stages.explanation: Santiago has a flock, a living, and familiar paths. Then a dream pulls him toward treasure in Egypt. Leaving could cost him the life he knows. Why would a writer spend time on his sheep? In Paulo Coelho’s The Alchemist, concrete details help us think about difficult choices. A symbol is a person, object, place, or action that suggests an idea beyond its literal role. Start with what it actually does; then explain the connection.
modelRows: Scene · original paraphrase
Santiago’s sheep follow him for food and water. He notices their repeated routines and dependence on him. He cares for them, but considers leaving to pursue treasure.
Detail → meaning
The sheep follow familiar routines → they can suggest the security, and limits, of a life without questioning what comes next. Their behaviour supports this reading.
Complete explanation

The sheep are real animals that provide Santiago with a living. Because their daily needs and routines keep them following a familiar path, they can also symbolize comfortable dependence. Leaving them makes his choice of uncertainty visible.
A memorable mistake
“The sheep symbolize symbolism.” The label explains nothing. Repair it with a link: “Their repeated routines suggest the comfort of a familiar life.” A symbol needs evidence, not a secret dictionary.
stages.model:
Scene · original paraphrase: Santiago’s sheep follow him for food and water. He notices their repeated routines and dependence on him. He cares for them, but considers leaving to pursue treasure.

Detail → meaning: The sheep follow familiar routines → they can suggest the security, and limits, of a life without questioning what comes next. Their behaviour supports this reading.

Complete explanation: The sheep are real animals that provide Santiago with a living. Because their daily needs and routines keep them following a familiar path, they can also symbolize comfortable dependence. Leaving them makes his choice of uncertainty visible.

A memorable mistake: “The sheep symbolize symbolism.” The label explains nothing. Repair it with a link: “Their repeated routines suggest the comfort of a familiar life.” A symbol needs evidence, not a secret dictionary.

questions.prompt: Scene: Santiago’s sheep follow him to food and water and repeat the same routines. Which explanation connects their behaviour to a symbolic meaning?
options: They are sheep, so they must symbolize innocence in every scene.
They provide wool and sometimes meat; that is the whole symbolic explanation.
Their repeated routines can suggest comfortable dependence on a familiar life.
answers: Their repeated routines can suggest comfortable dependence on a familiar life.
questions.hint: Find both a concrete behaviour and the idea that behaviour makes plausible.
questions.explanation: A supported symbolic reading connects what a detail does in this scene with a larger idea. Naming its practical use alone is literal description.

alternate.prompt: New detail: Santiago’s recurring dream points toward treasure at the distant Egyptian pyramids and encourages him to leave home. Which explanation links this detail to a symbolic meaning?
options: The distant pyramids can represent a goal that draws him beyond his familiar life.
The pyramids are buildings in Egypt, which fully explains their symbolic role.
All tall buildings always represent pride.
answers: The distant pyramids can represent a goal that draws him beyond his familiar life.

questions.prompt: Scene: Santiago’s sheep provide his livelihood and follow familiar routines. A reader says they symbolize comfortable security. What does that claim mean?
options: They are imaginary animals that exist only inside Santiago’s mind.
They must have exactly one meaning in every part of the novel.
They remain real animals in the story while also suggesting an idea.
answers: They remain real animals in the story while also suggesting an idea.
questions.hint: A symbolic reading adds a layer to the literal story.
questions.explanation: A symbol does not erase an object’s literal role or lock it into one universal meaning.

alternate.prompt: New detail: the Egyptian pyramids are a real destination in Santiago’s search and can suggest a distant ambition. What does this symbolic reading require?
options: Keeping their literal role as a destination while explaining the larger idea.
Treating the pyramids as imaginary because they carry meaning.
Assuming every pyramid in every story means ambition.
answers: Keeping their literal role as a destination while explaining the larger idea.

stages.title: Supply the link, not just the label
stages.explanation: Now try the explaining yourself. Use this small pattern: detail → possible meaning → because. “Because” makes you show your reasoning. A symbol can have more than one supported meaning, but not just any meaning. Use the scene to test your interpretation; do not rely on the colour or shape of an object alone.
modelRows: New scene · original paraphrase

After losing his money in Tangier, Santiago works in a crystal shop. He proposes an outdoor display to attract customers. The merchant fears that passers-by will break the glasses. He eventually agrees, and the display helps business.
One move missing
Claim: the fragile crystal can suggest the risks of change. Evidence: the merchant fears putting it outside, but the display attracts customers. Missing: explain HOW this evidence supports the claim.
Keep the claim proportionate
Crystal is literally merchandise that can break. Reading its fragility as a symbol is an interpretation supported by the merchant’s fear; the novel does not give us a rule that all glass means fear.
stages.model:
New scene · original paraphrase: After losing his money in Tangier, Santiago works in a crystal shop. He proposes an outdoor display to attract customers. The merchant fears that passers-by will break the glasses. He eventually agrees, and the display helps business.

One move missing: Claim: the fragile crystal can suggest the risks of change. Evidence: the merchant fears putting it outside, but the display attracts customers. Missing: explain HOW this evidence supports the claim.

Keep the claim proportionate: Crystal is literally merchandise that can break. Reading its fragility as a symbol is an interpretation supported by the merchant’s fear; the novel does not give us a rule that all glass means fear.

questions.prompt: Crystal-shop scene: the merchant fears an outdoor display will break his fragile glasses; he agrees, and it attracts customers. Which missing explanation best supports “the crystal can suggest the risks of change”?
options: The crystal is expensive, so every change will definitely make the merchant rich.
The display is outside the shop, so the scene is only about where furniture belongs.
Moving the fragile glasses exposes something valuable to possible loss, but keeping them protected would also miss an opportunity.
answers: Moving the fragile glasses exposes something valuable to possible loss, but keeping them protected would also miss an opportunity.
questions.hint: Connect possible damage and possible benefit to the choice about change.
questions.explanation: The explanation links a physical risk to a human decision without claiming that taking risks always succeeds.

alternate.prompt: New scene: Santiago can keep his flock and familiar livelihood or sell the sheep to fund the uncertain search for treasure. Which explanation best supports “selling the flock can symbolize accepting risk”?
options: He gives up a dependable source of income to make an uncertain goal possible.
Selling animals proves that he no longer values anything familiar.
Receiving money means the decision has no cost or uncertainty.
answers: He gives up a dependable source of income to make an uncertain goal possible.

rehearsal.prompt: Write the ONE missing move in 1–2 sentences. Claim: the fragile crystal can suggest the risks of change. Evidence: the merchant fears the outdoor display will cause breakage, but it later attracts customers. Explain how this evidence supports the claim. Then compare with the sample.
rehearsal.sample: Putting fragile goods outside risks damage but creates an opportunity. The crystal makes the merchant’s fear of losing something valuable concrete. Compare: did you explain the link, rather than repeat “it is symbolic”?

questions.prompt: Scene: after a theft in Tangier, Santiago works at the crystal shop and earns money that can let him continue. Which interpretation stays within this evidence?
options: The shop proves that every theft is secretly helpful to its victim.
The shop means Santiago’s dream has already come true.
The shop can represent a place of recovery where practical work makes renewed hope possible.
answers: The shop can represent a place of recovery where practical work makes renewed hope possible.
questions.hint: Choose a claim about this character’s recovery, not a guarantee about everyone’s suffering.
questions.explanation: Interpretation should fit the supplied events. Santiago rebuilds his resources; that does not make theft good or guarantee success.

alternate.prompt: New scene: Santiago leaves a familiar livelihood with his sheep to search for treasure, although the outcome is uncertain. Which interpretation stays within this evidence?
options: Leaving the flock can represent choosing uncertainty in pursuit of a goal.
Leaving the flock proves familiar work has no value for anyone.
His departure guarantees that every dream will come true.
answers: Leaving the flock can represent choosing uncertainty in pursuit of a goal.

rehearsal.prompt: Now remove more support. Using the theft → shop work → renewed resources sequence in the question, write one sentence naming a possible meaning for the shop and explaining it with evidence. Then compare.
rehearsal.sample: The shop can symbolize recovery because Santiago’s work there rebuilds the resources he lost and makes another attempt possible. A different meaning is reasonable if the same scene supports it.

stages.title: Connect a pattern across the story
stages.explanation: One symbol is a meaningful detail. An allegory is a story, or sustained story pattern, whose characters, places, and actions also develop a connected meaning beyond the literal events. You can read Santiago’s journey as an allegory of pursuing a purpose: leaving security, facing setbacks, and learning to act. “Personal Legend” is the novel’s name for a person’s calling or life purpose. A theme is the broader idea; allegory is how the story embodies it.
modelRows: Literal sequence
Santiago leaves his flock, loses his money in Tangier, then works in the crystal shop and rebuilds his resources. These are linked events, not a list of decorative objects.
Corresponding ideas
Leaving the flock → risking familiar security. Losing his money → encountering a setback. Working and rebuilding → learning to respond through action.
Connected reading

Together, these events can dramatize the pursuit of a purpose as a process that demands risk and persistence, not just wishing. “Follow your dreams” names a theme; explaining how the events enact that idea develops an allegorical reading.
A limit
This is a supported reading, not a code that forces every detail to mean one thing. A character can serve an allegorical role and still have ordinary needs and mixed motives.
stages.model:
Literal sequence: Santiago leaves his flock, loses his money in Tangier, then works in the crystal shop and rebuilds his resources. These are linked events, not a list of decorative objects.

Corresponding ideas: Leaving the flock → risking familiar security. Losing his money → encountering a setback. Working and rebuilding → learning to respond through action.

Connected reading: Together, these events can dramatize the pursuit of a purpose as a process that demands risk and persistence, not just wishing. “Follow your dreams” names a theme; explaining how the events enact that idea develops an allegorical reading.

A limit: This is a supported reading, not a code that forces every detail to mean one thing. A character can serve an allegorical role and still have ordinary needs and mixed motives.

questions.prompt: Sequence: Santiago leaves his flock, loses money in Tangier, then rebuilds his resources through shop work. Which statement develops an allegorical reading of this sequence?
options: The flock symbolizes security; no other event needs to be considered.
First he leaves, then he loses money, then he works.
Leaving security, meeting a setback, and rebuilding connect his travels to the difficult process of pursuing a purpose.
answers: Leaving security, meeting a setback, and rebuilding connect his travels to the difficult process of pursuing a purpose.
questions.hint: Look for several connected events AND a broader human process.
questions.explanation: An allegorical reading explains a sustained relationship between the literal sequence and a larger meaning. Plot summary or one symbol alone does not establish that relationship.

alternate.prompt: New sequence: the crystal merchant fears an outdoor display, permits it, and gains customers. Which statement develops an allegorical reading of this smaller pattern?
options: Fear, a cautious experiment, and a new opportunity can enact the process of learning to accept change.
The display stands outside the shop and brings customers.
Crystal is fragile, so we need no explanation of the merchant’s changing decisions.
answers: Fear, a cautious experiment, and a new opportunity can enact the process of learning to accept change.

rehearsal.prompt: Explain the pattern yourself in two sentences: how do leaving the flock AND rebuilding after the theft help turn Santiago’s journey into an allegory of pursuing a purpose? Use both events, then compare.
rehearsal.sample: Leaving the flock makes the cost of beginning visible: Santiago gives up familiar security. Rebuilding after the theft shows that pursuing a purpose also requires responding to setbacks, so the journey enacts a process of growth rather than an effortless wish.

questions.prompt: A classmate writes, “The lesson is that people need courage.” You have the sequence of Santiago leaving his flock and rebuilding after the theft. What must the classmate add to explain allegory rather than only state a theme?
options: Replace “courage” with the word “allegory” and keep everything else.
List more objects without explaining their connection.
Explain how the departure and recovery together enact that idea about courage.
answers: Explain how the departure and recovery together enact that idea about courage.
questions.hint: How does the story make the general idea happen through actions?
questions.explanation: A theme states an idea; an allegorical explanation maps the story’s connected actions onto that idea.

alternate.prompt: New scene: the merchant first fears a display, then tries it and gains customers. A reader writes, “Change can create opportunities.” What addition makes this an allegorical explanation?
options: Connect his fear, his decision to try, and the result to the broader process of accepting change.
Say “the story is symbolic” without using its events.
Describe the colour of the glasses, which the supplied scene does not specify.
answers: Connect his fear, his decision to try, and the result to the broader process of accepting change.

image.alt: At left, a flock is paired with a sheltered home to suggest familiar security. At right, linked scenes show departure, crystal-shop work, and onward travel, suggesting a connected process of risk, recovery, and growth.
image.caption: Compare one detail with the connected path: a symbol suggests an idea; an allegorical pattern develops an idea through linked events. The home, thread, and lower icons are teaching metaphors, not extra events in the novel. AI-generated illustration.

final.title: Help a reader see both layers
final.prompt: A classmate understands what happens but asks, “How is this more than an adventure?” Choose A or B from the source card. Write one paragraph of about 90–130 words. Explain one possible symbol using a concrete detail; then connect at least two events or choices to explain an allegorical idea about pursuing a purpose. Make the connection explicit with “because” or an equivalent explanation. Keep the literal events accurate. Use your own words; quotations, page numbers, and outside research are not required. After feedback, revise the least clear link. Different interpretations can succeed when the supplied evidence supports them.
final.source:
Paulo Coelho, The Alchemist, translated into English by Alan R. Clarke; scenes from Parts One and Two, before the desert journey. These are original teaching paraphrases, not quotations. All information needed for either option is below. The source link identifies the novel; use this card to write.

A · Guidance and choice. The old king gives Santiago two stones, Urim and Thummim, to help him seek yes/no guidance when he cannot understand omens (signs he interprets as guidance). The king also urges him to make his own decisions when possible. After the theft in Tangier, Santiago turns to the stones for reassurance. When both fall through a hole in his pouch, he picks them up and recalls his promise to decide for himself. He keeps the stones, feels less desperate, and begins to see the unfamiliar place as somewhere he can explore.

B · A dream kept at a distance. The crystal merchant wants to make a pilgrimage, a religious journey, to Mecca. He says imagining the journey helps him endure his repeated daily work, yet he fears having nothing left to live for once the dream is fulfilled. He has postponed leaving the shop. By contrast, after earning enough at the shop to buy sheep again, Santiago chooses to continue toward Egypt. Both men value a dream, but they respond differently to the possibility of acting on it. Interpret these individual choices; the merchant does not represent all Muslims or all religious believers.
rubric: Accurate evidence: Uses concrete details from chosen card A or B without invented quotations or events. At least two connected events or choices must be identifiable; paraphrase is sufficient. Do not require outside knowledge, a page citation, or strict word count.

Symbol and explanation: Identifies a concrete object, place, or action and explains a plausible meaning through what it does in the supplied scene. For A, stones may suggest guidance, reassurance, or the limits of dependence; for B, the dreamed-of pilgrimage or continued shop routine may suggest sustaining hope or postponement. Accept other grounded readings. Literal role must remain intact.

Allegorical connection: Explains how at least two events or choices together enact a broader process or tension about pursuing a purpose, rather than merely retelling events or naming a theme. A can connect receiving guidance with reclaiming decisions while retaining reassurance. B can connect the merchant’s postponement with Santiago’s decision to continue, showing competing responses to dreams. No single prescribed moral is required.

Clear reasoning: Makes the evidence-to-meaning connections understandable with because or equivalent causal reasoning; distinguishes a detail’s symbolic meaning from the sustained allegorical pattern. Accept accessible language and multilingual grammar when meaning is clear. Avoid universal claims about a religion or guaranteed success. Feedback must identify a response-grounded strength and one actionable next move without rewriting the paragraph; compare drafts only when available and only where evidence shows change.
final.delayedCheck: Next class, without reopening the models: a new scene from The Alchemist shows the Englishman studying alchemy through books while Santiago learns by observing the caravan and desert. In three sentences, suggest what the books might symbolize, explain that meaning using the scene, and connect the two ways of learning into a possible allegorical idea about pursuing understanding. title: Argument 1: Build a defensible case with Toulmin
objective: Construct and revise a phone-policy argument whose claim, grounds, warrant, backing, qualification and response to an exception work together.

stages.title: A fact does not walk itself to a conclusion
stages.explanation: Jia loses her place each time a phone lights up nearby. Arun keeps his phone ready because his ride home changes without warning. At a fictional student council meeting, both ask to be heard. “Phones distract students. Therefore, ban them all day.” The conclusion has sprinted ahead of its evidence. First learn the common pattern: make a claim, provide grounds, and explain the warrant connecting them. Then test its limits.
modelRows: Claim — what should we accept?
During independent reading, students should normally silence phones and put them out of sight. This is a contestable recommendation with a defined setting.
Grounds — what supports it?

Invented observation: during one reading period, several students stopped reading when nearby phones lit up. This supports a concern about interruption; it does not show that every student is distracted all day.
Warrant — why does that support the claim?
When avoidable notifications interrupt a shared reading task, a limited rule reducing those interruptions is justified. This connects an observation to a policy judgment; the reader may challenge it.
Read the bridge

Evidence is one shore; the claim is the other. The warrant connects them. Backing supports that connection. A real argument is not a proof by picture: a bridge can look sturdy while its underlying assumption is disputable.

stages.title: Support the bridge, then test its limits
stages.explanation: A warrant is not automatically true because we have named it. Backing gives a reason to accept that connecting principle. A qualifier sets the claim’s scope or strength. In Toulmin analysis, rebuttal identifies conditions where the inference may not hold. In writing, acknowledge that challenge and explain whether it changes, limits, or defeats your claim.
modelRows: Backing — why accept this warrant?

For the limited-restriction warrant, one ethical justification is that each student has an equal claim to uninterrupted learning time; protecting one person’s convenience should not repeatedly remove that opportunity from others. This supports the principle. It is reasoning, not another invented statistic.
Qualifier — how far does the claim hold?
“Normally, during independent reading” limits when the recommendation applies. “Maybe phones are bad” merely sounds hesitant without defining a useful boundary.
Rebuttal condition → response

A student may need an agreed accessibility tool or urgent contact. That exception challenges a blanket rule. Permit approved access and establish a contact route, then assess whether these arrangements actually work.
A complete model

During independent reading, students should normally silence and put away phones. In our invented observation, nearby alerts interrupted reading. Avoidable interruptions to a shared task justify a proportionate restriction because each learner deserves a fair chance to concentrate. However, agreed accessibility uses require exceptions; the rule should target unnecessary alerts, not necessary access.
Six components, not six paragraphs
Claim + grounds + warrant + backing + qualifier + rebuttal conditions are reasoning jobs. A sentence can do more than one job, and their order can vary with the audience.

stages.title: Build, challenge, revise
stages.explanation: Now put the components to work. Begin with a map, then write connected prose. Use the evidence packet below without pretending it settles every question. Your claim can favor stricter or more flexible restrictions. The test is whether your evidence, reasoning and qualifications fit together. Save your final response: Lesson 2 will reuse its claim and warrant.
modelRows: Research A

Research A — Louis-Philippe Beland and Richard Murphy, 2015 research summary, LSE. Their study of schools in four English cities compared test-score changes around phone bans and found gains, especially among lower-achieving students. This was not a randomized experiment. It does not establish the effect of a particular policy at our school. Original: https://blogs.lse.ac.uk/politicsandpolicy/phone-home-should-mobiles-be-banned-in-schools/
Research B

Research B — Victoria A. Goodyear and colleagues, SMART Schools, 2025. In an observational comparison of 1,227 pupils aged 12–15 at 30 English schools, restrictive policies were associated with less phone use during school, but not better mental wellbeing or less overall phone use. A comparison at one period cannot establish that the policy caused these outcomes. Original: https://research.birmingham.ac.uk/files/256423016/GoodyearVA2025School.pdf
Evidence discipline
These studies differ in date, methods and outcomes. Test-score gains and the absence of a wellbeing difference are not the same claim. Neither study tests our exact proposed policy.
Pair repair — one move missing

Claim: trial a reading-time restriction. Grounds: Research A suggests some academic benefits from bans elsewhere. Warrant: credible evidence of possible learning benefits can justify a limited, reviewable trial. Backing: a reversible trial can gather local evidence while limiting the cost of a mistaken decision. Missing: a qualification acknowledging what this study cannot establish.
From map to prose
Move from a defined recommendation to relevant grounds, explain the warrant, support a contestable assumption, then handle limits and exceptions. Do not write six disconnected definitions.

final.title: Your council recommendation: a new decision
final.prompt: The council now asks whether to extend a reading-time phone restriction to independent study periods. This is a fresh decision, not the model’s reading rule. Choose a position. First make a six-part Toulmin map using the headings Claim, Grounds, Warrant, Backing, Qualifier, and Rebuttal/response. Then write a connected 120–180-word recommendation to the council. Use at least one research card and one relevant scenario detail; name their limits and do not present invented details as research. Address a real exception. After feedback, revise one weak connection and add: “I changed ___ because ___.” Save or copy the final version and map for Lesson 2. In the next lesson you will turn your warrant into a criterion and expand this case into a whole-argument outline.

NEW INVENTED SCENARIO: Independent study includes silent reading, collaborative tasks and occasional teacher-approved phone tools. Some students need reliable pickup updates. The council can trial a rule for two weeks and review it; no local outcome data have yet been collected. You may propose conditions, but label them proposals, not existing facts.
rubric: Claim and scope: Gives a contestable recommendation about independent study, with a meaningful condition or degree of certainty; either position is acceptable. Map and prose need not use identical wording.

Grounds and accuracy: Uses at least one credited research finding and one scenario detail accurately. Distinguishes invented scenario facts from research and avoids a causal guarantee or unsupported local result.

Warrant and backing: Explains how the evidence supports the recommendation and supplies a reason to accept that connecting principle. Backing may be ethical reasoning or relevant evidence, not necessarily a second citation. Do not reward labels without reasoning.

Exception and response: Identifies a plausible limiting condition or serious objection and responds concretely through a justified exception, changed claim, or reasoned defense. Does not dismiss accessibility or contact needs.

Connected argument: Map contains all six jobs and prose connects them into a defensible line of reasoning. Word range is guidance, not a rigid gate. On revision identify a specific demonstrated change without inventing improvement.

title: Argument 2: Organize and weigh a criteria-based case
objective: Expand your Lesson 1 Toulmin argument into a complete criteria-based outline that justifies its standards, applies evidence and weighs a serious trade-off.

stages.title: Bring yesterday’s reasoning into today’s structure
stages.explanation: Reopen your saved Argument 1 map and recommendation. Keep them beside this lesson; they are not imported automatically. Jia and Arun still disagree, even after both offer evidence. They disagree about what a good rule must accomplish. Today you will build a complete argument by making those standards explicit. A criterion is a standard for judgment; a reason says why a particular option meets it.
modelRows: Retrieve Lesson 1

Copy your claim and warrant. Underline the value inside the warrant: learning, autonomy, fair access, or another defensible concern. If your work is unfinished, reconstruct your own six-part map from the supplied source card before continuing.
Warrant → criterion

Yesterday: “Avoidable interruptions to a shared task justify a proportionate restriction.” Today: “A good phone policy should protect sustained participation in learning.” The criterion turns the underlying value into an explicit standard for comparing policies.
Make it usable

Learning: compare interruptions and participation during learning tasks, not just how many phones are confiscated. Autonomy: compare how much unnecessary restriction each option imposes outside learning tasks. Fair access: check whether students can use necessary tools and reliable urgent-contact arrangements.
Justify the standard

Learning matters because the school must make instruction accessible. Autonomy matters because students need opportunities to make responsible choices. Fair access matters because a rule should not exclude students who need tools or contact arrangements. These are arguments the audience can question.
Memorable mistake → repair

“Policy A wins because my criterion is being Policy A.” That is a preference wearing a name badge. Repair: define a standard either policy could meet, apply it consistently, and justify why it matters.

stages.title: Build the complete argument in five moves
stages.explanation: Here is today’s whole-argument structure: frame and thesis → justify criteria → apply criteria → engage the strongest challenge → weigh and qualify. These are five rhetorical moves, not a compulsory five-paragraph essay. Each application uses yesterday’s Toulmin reasoning. A longer essay may spend several paragraphs applying one criterion; a short argument may combine moves.
modelRows: 1 · Frame + thesis

Decision: whether to restrict phones throughout the school day. Model position: trial a lesson-time restriction with necessary exceptions before adopting a full-day restriction. This answers the question and defines the scope.
2 · Establish + justify criteria
Judge the options by learning participation, autonomy and fair access. Explain why those standards matter to students and teachers before using them to declare a winner.
3 · Apply with Toulmin

Claim: a lesson-time policy preserves more break-time choice. Grounds: the invented option explicitly permits lunch use; the full-day option does not. Warrant: permitting a choice outside instruction better serves autonomy when no relevant harm is shown. Backing: restrictions need reasons proportionate to the freedom removed. Limit: choice alone does not establish better learning.
4 · Engage the strongest challenge

Full-day supporters may argue that lunch use carries distractions into lessons. That challenges whether the flexible option protects learning. Take it seriously; compare the evidence and propose what local review would need to check.
5 · Weigh + qualify

Model conclusion: initially prefer a lesson-time trial because it targets the demonstrated concern while preserving other choices, but reconsider if local evidence shows continuing learning disruption. This is a reasoned priority, not a claim that autonomy always wins.

stages.title: When the criteria disagree
stages.explanation: “A wins two criteria; B wins one. Case closed.” Not yet. One serious access problem may matter more than two minor conveniences. Weighing explains why a consideration deserves priority in this situation. Compare the size, likelihood and distribution of effects, and ask whether an option can be changed to reduce its costs. Do not invent a numerical score to hide a judgment.
modelRows: Practice options — invented

A: phones stored for the full school day, with a stated accessibility exception. B: phones away during instruction but available at lunch, with the same exception. A could simplify expectations; B preserves more choice. These are design features and possible consequences, not measured effects.
Strong challenge
“Your flexible policy allows habits that undermine later attention.” A serious response needs evidence about that effect or a plan to investigate it, rather than saying the opponent hates freedom.
A weighed response

If the learning benefit of a full-day restriction is uncertain, the definite loss of break-time choice needs stronger justification. Prefer a reviewable lesson-time trial initially, with reliable necessary access. If the trial leaves substantial disruption, greater restriction may be justified.
A defensible alternative

A writer could favor a full-day trial if they justify why consistent expectations are likely to protect learning and establish reliable exceptions. The strength of the reasoning, not which option wins, determines the quality.
Carry the work forward

Keep the evidence-to-claim connection from Lesson 1. Add justified standards, consistent comparisons and an explicit priority. In your final paragraph, explain what you concede, why your priority still holds, and what would change your conclusion.

Claim that one problem proves no school rule should exist.
answers: Treat it as a serious challenge, revise the rule or judgment, and explain how it changes the weighing.
questions.hint: Qualification is responsiveness to evidence, not a sign of defeat.
questions.explanation: A defensible judgment changes when a condition supporting it fails.

alternate.prompt: Fresh task: a preferred library schedule excludes the only available bus group. What should an evaluator do?
options: Reconsider the access judgment and test a modification before reaffirming the conclusion.
Rename exclusion as access.
Delete the access criterion without explanation.
answers: Reconsider the access judgment and test a modification before reaffirming the conclusion.

final.title: Build on your first argument: the council’s pilot review
final.prompt: Begin by copying your Lesson 1 claim and warrant under “Starting point.” Then use the NEW invented pilot evidence below to revisit the whole-school phone question. You may keep, modify or reverse your earlier position. Produce a five-part outline: (1) frame the decision and state a qualified thesis; (2) define and justify two or three criteria; (3) apply the SAME criteria to A and B, using evidence plus explicit warrants; (4) address the strongest challenge; (5) weigh the trade-offs and reach a qualified judgment. Include at least one research card alongside the pilot evidence, with an appropriate limitation. Then develop a 120–180-word trade-off paragraph explaining what you concede, which consideration deserves priority and why, and what would change your judgment. After feedback, revise the weakest connection and add: “Compared with Lesson 1, I now ___ because ___.” A complete essay is not required. Either policy or a justified modification can be defended.
final.source:
All named students, local observations, pilot figures and policy options in this lesson are invented classroom scenarios, not findings about our school. Research A and B are credited paraphrases of real studies. Do not turn a scenario into a research claim.

Research A — Louis-Philippe Beland and Richard Murphy, 2015 research summary, LSE. Their study of schools in four English cities compared test-score changes around phone bans and found gains, especially among lower-achieving students. This was not a randomized experiment. It does not establish the effect of a particular policy at our school. Original: https://blogs.lse.ac.uk/politicsandpolicy/phone-home-should-mobiles-be-banned-in-schools/

Research B — Victoria A. Goodyear and colleagues, SMART Schools, 2025. In an observational comparison of 1,227 pupils aged 12–15 at 30 English schools, restrictive policies were associated with less phone use during school, but not better mental wellbeing or less overall phone use. A comparison at one period cannot establish that the policy caused these outcomes. Original: https://research.birmingham.ac.uk/files/256423016/GoodyearVA2025School.pdf

NEW INVENTED PILOT — NOT REAL RESEARCH: The council compares two different year groups over two weeks; neither group was randomly assigned, and there is no before-policy baseline. A stores phones all day; B keeps phones away during instruction but permits lunch use. Both officially allow necessary accessibility use. Teachers recorded 3 phone interruptions per 20 lessons under A and 5 per 20 under B. A required approximately 10 minutes of collection/return time each day; B approximately 3 minutes of reminders. Two students under A reported delays obtaining approved accessibility access; none were reported under B. These are small, incomplete observations, not proof of causation. No learning achievement, long-term wellbeing or autonomy survey was measured. The council can modify either option and extend the trial. Do not invent missing data.

If your Lesson 1 response is unavailable, reconstruct a six-part map from these source cards first; use your reconstructed claim and warrant as the starting point.
rubric: Continuity and structure: Includes a Lesson 1 starting claim and warrant (or explicitly reconstructed version) and a complete five-move outline. Position may change; no cross-lesson automatic retrieval is assumed. Flexible paragraph counts are acceptable.
Justified criteria: Defines two or three relevant, usable standards and explains why each matters; criteria do not merely encode a preferred policy. Applies the same standards to both options.

Evidence and warrants: Uses pilot details and at least one research card accurately; explains their connection to criterion judgments. Distinguishes invented pilot from real research and recognizes nonrandom groups/no baseline and limits on transfer. Does not claim unmeasured learning gains.
Challenge and response: Addresses a strong opposing consideration fairly and offers a reasoned response, qualification or modification rather than dismissing an opposing viewpoint.

Weighing and qualified judgment: Developed paragraph compares competing considerations, justifies priority in this context, and identifies a plausible condition for reconsideration. Counting criteria or repeating the thesis is insufficient. Either option or modification may succeed; do not enforce the model’s preference.
final.delayedCheck: Next class, without the model, reconstruct the five moves. New issue: should group projects use one shared grade or separate individual grades? Justify two criteria, explain one evidence-to-criterion warrant, and write two sentences weighing collaboration against individual accountability. Do not reuse phone-policy claims.

title: Annotated Bibliography Part 2
objective: Write and revise a first source annotation that accurately summarizes an idea, tests the source’s evidence, and connects it to a specific scene and tentative answer.

stages.title: Summarize the idea you came for
stages.explanation: You tell your partner that Beowulf’s life matters because he wins. They point to the moment he wins and dies. Your MLA citation lets them find Debamitra Kar’s chapter. The annotation lets them see what you learned from it, what you trust, and whether your answer needs to change.
stages.model:
Set up the research — Question — How do Beowulf and The Epic of Gilgamesh define a lasting achievement? My first guess is that both heroes want to be remembered for their victories. I think public recognition is what makes their lives feel meaningful.

Citation already in place — Kar, Debamitra. “Beowulf.” English Literature up to 1590, ebooks.inflibnet.ac.in/engp01/chapter/beowulf/. The annotation below focuses on the chapter’s discussion of leadership and Hrothgar’s speech.

Summarize — Kar reads Beowulf as a poem that uses its heroes’ speeches to ask what makes a good leader. After Beowulf defeats Grendel’s mother, Hrothgar warns him that strength is temporary and that pride can distort how a leader sees himself. On Kar’s reading, this speech makes the victory an occasion to think about how a warrior should use his power.

Evaluate — Kar quotes the speech directly, so I can check how Hrothgar moves from praise to a warning about age and death. That shift supports Kar’s claim that the poem uses speeches to teach about leadership. The example is persuasive about what Hrothgar teaches here. I would need to examine Beowulf’s later choices to see how far the lesson explains his career as king.

Connect — I would compare Hrothgar’s warning after the fight with Gilgamesh’s return to Uruk, when his attention turns to the city wall. My first answer emphasized being remembered for winning. These scenes make me ask whether a hero earns a lasting reputation by doing something that helps his people after his own strength is gone.

Kar reads Hrothgar’s warning as a lesson about leadership.

I will compare two halls.
The critic sees the empty hall as a sign that power can collapse.

rehearsal.prompt: Say or write one sentence beginning “Kar reads the warning as…” Put the idea in your own words, then compare.
rehearsal.sample: Kar sees the warning as a lesson for a successful warrior about the limits of his power.

questions.prompt: What should you write down when saving a quotation from a source?
options: Exact words, who said them, the page or section, and enough context to check the meaning.
The sentence and the search-engine result title.
The exact words and your own interpretation alone.
answers: Exact words, who said them, the page or section, and enough context to check the meaning.
questions.hint: Could a partner find the words and tell who actually spoke?
questions.explanation: A source may quote the novel or a character. Keep that voice distinct from the critic’s and verify literary quotations in your edition.

alternate.prompt: A PDF quotes a translation of Gilgamesh. What should your notes capture?
options: The wording and the PDF file name.
The wording, speaker, translation if identified, and where to verify the passage.
Only the article author’s surname.
answers: The wording, speaker, translation if identified, and where to verify the passage.

stages.title: Evaluate the evidence behind a claim
stages.explanation: “This source is extremely credible because it looks extremely credible.” That review could describe a menu. Give the reader something they can check. Name one claim, point to the author’s evidence, and explain what it supports and where its reach ends.
stages.model:
Claim + evidence — Kar says the poem teaches leadership through speeches. Hrothgar’s warning that strength fades gives Kar something specific to point to.

What it supports — A warning delivered just after a victory supports the idea that a hero needs guidance even at his strongest.

Where it stops — A speech shows what Hrothgar urges. To judge whether Beowulf lives by it, check what he does later. A limitation can be about the reach of the evidence.

questions.prompt: Which evaluation explains why the evidence matters?
options: The chapter is reliable because its writer has a title.
The chapter uses a speech and therefore proves its whole argument.
The warning about fading strength supports Kar’s reading of this speech as advice about power.
answers: The warning about fading strength supports Kar’s reading of this speech as advice about power.
questions.hint: Pair the precise detail with the precise claim it supports.
questions.explanation: The warning directly supports a reading of the speech. A title or a quotation by itself tells us less.

alternate.prompt: A scholar says Enkidu’s death changes Gilgamesh’s priorities. Which evaluation tests the evidence?
options: The move from seeking fame to seeking survival after the death supports the proposed shift.
The scholar knows more about the epic than I do.
One death proves that grief explains all of Gilgamesh’s actions.
answers: The move from seeking fame to seeking survival after the death supports the proposed shift.

questions.prompt: How far does the evidence about the funeral reach?
options: It establishes that Beowulf’s people praise him publicly, while leaving his private motives open.
It proves that Beowulf always fought for praise.
It gives us no evidence about reputation.
answers: It establishes that Beowulf’s people praise him publicly, while leaving his private motives open.
questions.hint: Whose words are we hearing at the funeral?
questions.explanation: The mourners’ praise shows public reputation. Their words give limited access to the hero’s motives.

alternate.prompt: People celebrate a hero’s return. What can their celebration establish?
options: The hero acted only to win their approval.
The community values the deed, while the hero’s own reasons remain open.
The hero’s deed solved every problem.
answers: The community values the deed, while the hero’s own reasons remain open.

rehearsal.prompt: Try one missing move. Claim: the funeral makes reputation public. Evidence: the mourners praise Beowulf aloud. Supply the limit in one sentence, then compare.
rehearsal.sample: The praise shows how the mourners remember him. His own reasons for fighting need evidence from another scene.

image.caption: Test what the underlined evidence can show. Then explain how that finding helps you read a specific scene. AI-generated illustration.

stages.title: Connect the source to a scene and your answer
stages.explanation: Your reader needs to see where the idea could enter your essay. Name the scene, say what the source helps you notice there, and decide how that affects your tentative answer. A source that makes you qualify your answer has earned its place.
stages.model:
From source to scene — Kar’s reading of the speech gives me a question to ask when Wiglaf joins the dragon fight. Does the scene reward individual courage, or does it show how much a leader depends on others?

From scene to answer — Wiglaf’s help complicates my claim that Beowulf’s meaningful achievement is an individual victory. I would compare his help with Enkidu joining Gilgamesh in the Cedar Forest.

Find sources — On scholar.google.com, search a title in quotation marks plus an idea: “Beowulf” kingship, “Epic of Gilgamesh” mortality, or “The Alchemist” “Paulo Coelho” fate. options: Kar is useful because my essay is also about Beowulf.
Kar’s focus on leadership helps me ask whether Wiglaf’s help complicates the idea that a hero succeeds alone.
Kar’s chapter could go in my second paragraph.
answers: Kar’s focus on leadership helps me ask whether Wiglaf’s help complicates the idea that a hero succeeds alone.
questions.hint: Look for a scene and the effect on an answer.
questions.explanation: Wiglaf’s action provides a place to test a specific idea about heroism.

options: The critic also discusses Santiago.
The article is useful for paragraph three.
I’ll use the hawk scene to ask whether purpose in The Alchemist comes from pursuing a dream or also from responding to danger facing others.
answers: I’ll use the hawk scene to ask whether purpose in The Alchemist comes from pursuing a dream or also from responding to danger facing others.

rehearsal.prompt: Try one missing move. Source idea: allies help heroes achieve their goals. Scene: Enkidu joins the expedition. My tentative answer: meaningful achievements are individual. Write the effect on my answer, then compare.
rehearsal.sample: Enkidu’s participation makes me qualify my answer: the expedition may bring Gilgamesh fame, but that achievement depends on shared effort.

questions.prompt: Which set fits the assignment if you compare Beowulf and The Alchemist?
options: Two Beowulf analyses and two plot summaries of The Alchemist.
Four sources that all repeat your tentative answer.
One analysis of each work, one useful historical source, and one philosophical source that challenges your answer.
answers: One analysis of each work, one useful historical source, and one philosophical source that challenges your answer.
questions.hint: Check coverage, source type and disagreement.
questions.explanation: This set covers both works with analysis, and one source puts pressure on the tentative answer.

alternate.prompt: A search result on Gilgamesh sounds perfect, but only its abstract is available. What should you do?
options: Find and read the full text or choose a readable source with evidence you can assess.
Annotate the abstract as though you read the article.
Use a plot summary to fill the gap.
answers: Find and read the full text or choose a readable source with evidence you can assess.

final.title: Write your first annotation
final.prompt:
Use Ira Spar’s source card and open his essay to check your evidence. Choose one question. A — What makes an achievement last in Gilgamesh and Beowulf? Start from the idea that great deeds earn lasting fame. B — How does facing a limit change what a hero values in Gilgamesh and The Alchemist? Start from the idea that a hero finds meaning by persisting until the original goal is achieved.

The MLA citation is supplied. Draft 150–200 words of annotation, with or without the labels Summarize, Evaluate and Connect. Explain Spar’s idea in your own words, test one specific claim against the evidence he gives, and name a limitation. Connect the idea to a specific scene and explain how it supports, challenges or refines the starting answer. Use the feedback to revise one sentence where you can make your reasoning more precise.

For submission, start with your own question, two literary works and a tentative answer of two or three sentences. Include four outside sources in alphabetical order by author (or title if unsigned), each with an MLA citation and 150–200 words of annotation. Include at least two literary analyses covering both works across the set, and at least one source that challenges or complicates your thinking. Test a specific claim in at least one entry. Read each source or the relevant chapter and identify its scope. Plot summaries can orient you. Keep them outside your four entries. Use at least three sources in the essay. Finish with a separate 150–200-word reflection in connected prose about how your answer changed, where sources differ, and what is still open and which passages you’ll revisit.
final.source:
Spar, Ira. “Gilgamesh.” Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History, The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Apr. 2009, www.metmuseum.org/essays/gilgamesh/.

Read the section from the recasting of Enkidu as companion through Gilgamesh’s return to Uruk. In that section, Spar argues that the later epic turns a reckless king’s quest into a lesson about what a mortal can leave behind. After Enkidu dies, Gilgamesh searches for a way to escape death. Uta-napishtim explains that mortals die. Spar points to the king’s attention to Uruk’s defensive wall on his return and reads it as a sign that achievements for his people and his god can outlast him. That reading interprets a detail in the ending. Check the wording of the final scene in your own translation to see how explicitly it shows a change of mind.

Scene reminders for comparison. A — In Beowulf’s final battle, Wiglaf helps defeat the dragon. The Geats later honor their king at his funeral. B — Near the end of The Alchemist, Santiago learns from a robber’s dream that the treasure may be back in Spain. He returns to the place where his journey began. These reminders are paraphrases.
rubric: Summarize accurately: Paraphrases Spar’s relevant interpretation about mortality, maturity or enduring accomplishments, with attribution and a clear sense of scope. Avoid rewarding a plot recap alone.

Evaluate evidence and limits: Names a specific claim and the evidence behind it, such as the narrative movement from Enkidu’s death through the failed quest to the wall. Explains how strongly a detail supports the claim and names a relevant limit. Credit a reason tied to Spar’s method or publication where explained, not prestige alone.

Connect to the research question: Explains how Spar’s interpretation helps examine a specific scene in one or both works and how it supports, complicates or revises the tentative answer. Accept either question and other grounded readings of the scenes.

Write a usable annotation: Aims for 150–200 words of coherent annotation beneath the supplied citation. Accept headings or connected prose. Assess original wording and attribution. Do not require retyping the citation, quoting, or completing the full bibliography and reflection here.
final.delayedCheck: Next class, try this with a source you have not annotated. Say its idea in your own words. Then complete “This detail supports the claim because …” and “I would test that idea against the moment when …” before checking your notes.

title: Copywork: Notice a Choice, Make a Choice
objective: Copy a short model accurately, explain the effect of specific wording, and transfer one writerly move into original writing.

stages.title: Copy slowly enough to see the choices
stages.explanation: A learner says, “I know what good writing looks like. I just cannot make mine do that.” Give the learner something small enough to study. In this 12–15 minute workshop, you will copy a short original paragraph, explain how a choice works, and transfer a move into new writing. Have paper and a pen ready. The copying is done on paper; the app checks your decisions and saves your final application.
stages.model: The clock swallowed our last minute. Around the table, pencils tapped, pages whispered, and one stubborn question refused to sit down. We had filled the board with answers; now we needed the courage to erase one. Maya raised her hand. For once, the smallest voice made the largest opening.

Your turn · 2 minutes

Copy this paragraph by hand, keeping its wording, punctuation, and sentence breaks. Compare your copy with the source and correct any differences. Typing is an accessible alternative when handwriting is not suitable.
Notice · 1 minute
Mark three specific choices: a word, a repeated pattern, or a change in sentence length. Draw a line from each observation to the exact wording.

options: Restore “swallowed” so you can study the author’s actual choice.
Keep the change because the main event is similar.
answers: Restore “swallowed” so you can study the author’s actual choice.

options: Leave it: both versions describe a gate.
Restore “groaned,” then investigate what its sound suggests.
answers: Restore “groaned,” then investigate what its sound suggests.

options: “Maya raised her hand” is short after a longer sentence.
The writer uses good language.
answers: “Maya raised her hand” is short after a longer sentence.
questions.hint: Point to words or a pattern another reader can locate.
questions.explanation: A precise observation gives your explanation evidence to work with.

options: There is a lot of description.
“Rattled” gives the rain a sharp, repeated sound.
answers: “Rattled” gives the rain a sharp, repeated sound.

stages.title: Explain what the choice makes the reader notice
stages.explanation: “The writer uses imagery. This creates an image. The image is very imagery-like.” The label has gone in a circle and arrived home exhausted. Explain instead what particular words make a reader picture, feel, or understand in this situation. Naming the technique is optional; showing how the wording works is essential.
stages.model: “Swallowed” turns time into a consuming force, making the unfinished discussion feel threatened by the clock.

“swallowed our last minute”
Effect
The verb makes time feel like a hungry opponent taking away a final opportunity.
Evidence → explanation
The verb “swallowed” makes the end of the discussion feel like a loss forced on the group.
Missing move · your turn

The question uses personification to interest the reader.
answers: “Refused to sit down” makes the question seem persistent, resisting an easy ending.

questions.explanation: Connect the exact action to the problem in the scene.

“Stood between” turns silence into a barrier separating the people.
answers: “Stood between” turns silence into a barrier separating the people.

rehearsal.prompt: Complete the missing explanation of the stubborn question in your own words.

Count the letters in both words.

questions.hint: What changes about Maya’s place in this group?
questions.explanation: A feature matters because of what it contributes to the moment.

options: State that full and empty are antonyms.
Explain how crowded surroundings sharpen the feeling of one person’s absence.
answers: Explain how crowded surroundings sharpen the feeling of one person’s absence.

stages.title: Borrow a move and make it your own
stages.explanation: Imitation is a deliberate experiment: borrow a useful choice, then make it serve new content. A copied sentence remains someone else’s wording and needs attribution. Your own experiment should develop a new observation, not merely disguise the source. For this workshop, a few sentences are enough; David’s full student assignment asks for two original paragraphs and two distinct moves.
stages.model: Model: “The clock swallowed our last minute.” Transfer: “The inbox swallowed my quiet morning.” The shared move gives an object a consuming action; the new sentence describes a different pressure.
modelRows: Complete model
The inbox swallowed my quiet morning. Giving the inbox an appetite makes incoming tasks feel like a force consuming time.
One support removed
A library closes just as someone finds a useful book. Write one sentence giving the closing building a purposeful action; then explain the effect you wanted.
Compare after trying
“The library pulled the evening out from under my research.” The action makes closing time feel like the removal of support. This is one possible experiment, not a sentence to reproduce.
Less support · 2 minutes
Choose a different classroom or everyday moment. Borrow contrast, sentence-length change, or personification. Write two sentences and explain the move.

questions.prompt: Which response demonstrates meaningful transfer of the “smallest/largest” contrast?
options: “The shortest message carried the heaviest news” uses contrast for a new emotional situation.
“The smallest voice made the largest opening” with Maya renamed Alex.
answers: “The shortest message carried the heaviest news” uses contrast for a new emotional situation.
questions.hint: Look for a changed meaning, not just a renamed character.
questions.explanation: Transfer makes the technique do new work.

alternate.prompt: Which transfers “The silence stood between them” into a new situation?
options: The same sentence with one person’s name changed.
“The unsigned form stood between her and the scholarship” makes paperwork a barrier.
answers: “The unsigned form stood between her and the scholarship” makes paperwork a barrier.

rehearsal.prompt: Write your own library-closing sentence and a brief explanation before comparing.
rehearsal.sample: “The library locked away the answer with its books.” The action makes closing time feel like losing access to a discovery.

questions.prompt: You have named three techniques in the model. How will you show you can use one?
options: Write an original example, identify the borrowed move, and explain its purpose.
Add three more technique labels to the model.
answers: Write an original example, identify the borrowed move, and explain its purpose.
questions.hint: The goal includes using a choice, not just recognizing it.
questions.explanation: A new example and its explanation make transfer visible.

alternate.prompt: After noticing repeated openings in a speech, what would show transfer?
options: List three synonyms for repetition.
Use repeated openings in a new appeal and explain what they emphasize.
answers: Use repeated openings in a new appeal and explain what they emphasize.

final.title: A fresh passage, then your own writing
final.prompt: Spend about 4 minutes, including one revision. Choose either passage below. Copy it on paper, compare carefully, and mark three specific choices. In the response box: (1) identify your chosen passage; (2) quote a short detail and explain its effect in context; (3) write 2–3 original sentences about a different situation, borrowing one move; (4) name that move and explain what it does in your new writing. Add a brief note confirming you compared your handwritten copy. The app cannot inspect handwriting, so check accuracy with a partner or David. Read the feedback and revise one specific part. This practice is not the full six-paragraph Canvas assignment.

Purpose of the move: Identifies the move in the new writing and explains what it helps the new reader notice or understand.

Copying reflection: States that the copied passage was compared with the source and mentions checking or correcting wording/punctuation; do not claim to verify handwriting or assess its accuracy from this text response.
final.delayedCheck: At your next planning session, take a different short passage from your own subject. Without reopening this lesson, copy two sentences, mark a choice, explain its effect, and try that choice in two new sentences. Compare your work with the routine afterward.
